profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at a university-affiliated reproductive health research center in early 1989, several months after the fall 1988 mail and telephone survey of outpatient voluntary sterilization services in Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico, Nevada, and Utah. The center is preparing a follow-up internal report for a funder briefing on how sterilization services are actually available across the Southwest, with particular attention to outpatient female sterilization, vasectomy pricing, referral patterns, and gaps affecting low-income patients. The immediate meeting is between the physician lead and the survey operations coordinator to decide how to handle the provider confirmation phase, what belongs in each state's working service map, who will update cost and referral entries, and what the first 'state summary draft' should contain. The agenda is to finalize the callback list, settle inclusion rules for procedure sites versus counseling-and-referral offices, assign responsibility for confirming unusual low-cost providers and cross-border referral routes, and align on the form of the first draft package. The expected outcome is an apparently shared plan for the follow-up calls, database updates, division of labor, and the initial set of state summaries.

members.name: Dr. Elaine Mercer
members.role: Medical Director for Reproductive Services Research
members.expertise: Family planning policy, outpatient sterilization practice patterns, interpretation of service availability data
members.background: An OB-GYN who has led regional access studies and regularly briefs public health groups on barriers to reproductive services, with particular attention to how patients actually obtain procedures across referral networks rather than how services appear in directories.
members.private_state: She wants the follow-up report to be useful for a near-term funder conversation about real patient access, especially for women facing high procedure costs, and she wants a concise but persuasive draft without reopening the entire survey design.
hidden_assumptions: A provider can reasonably be treated as offering sterilization if a patient begins care there and is routinely guided through a dependable referral path to the actual procedure site.
When discussing service availability for a state, the practical routes residents use matter more than whether every final procedure occurs inside state borders.
A quick confirmation call is enough if a knowledgeable contact indicates the provider's status and basic access pattern are still materially the same.
A state summary draft is primarily a short interpretive narrative with a few illustrative provider examples, cost notes, and access barriers for briefing purposes.
If unusual low-cost options are part of the patient pathway, they should appear in the summary even if they are exceptions rather than the dominant model.

members.name: Rafael Ortiz
members.expertise: Provider directory maintenance, mail and telephone survey follow-up, coding of health service records for regional studies
members.background: A public health research coordinator with experience running multi-state provider surveys, maintaining consistent provider files, and producing structured state-by-state inventories from mixed mail and phone follow-up data.
members.private_state: He wants a defensible, internally consistent database that can be converted into clean state summaries without special-case recoding, and he is trying to contain callback workload while preserving standard survey categories.
hidden_assumptions: A provider should count as offering sterilization only if the procedure itself is performed at that provider's listed outpatient site.
Service availability for a state means the in-state provider inventory for that state's section, while referral destinations outside the state can be mentioned separately if needed.
Confirming a provider's status means updating the standardized callback sheet with current fee, procedure type, and site-status fields, not just hearing that they are still active.
A state summary draft is the structured output normally built from the provider file: tables, coded listings, and concise notes ready for later narrative interpretation.
Special referral cases are useful annotations but should not reshape the core inventory categories unless the coding rules are explicitly changed.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a provider that 'offers' sterilization
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to identify the sites 'offering' female sterilization and vasectomy in each state.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means sites that function as the patient's access point for the service, including offices that counsel, arrange, and reliably channel patients to the procedure.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means sites where the sterilization procedure is actually performed under that provider's own listing.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In reproductive health discussions, 'offering' is routinely used as shorthand and sounds perfectly ordinary to both of them; the divergence sits in an unstated operational definition that each assumes is obvious.

misalignment_points.topic: Boundary of 'service availability for each state'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to map out the 'service availability for each state.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes each state's availability picture should include regular cross-border referral routes that residents actually use, such as low-cost options patients are sent to in California or Arizona.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes each state's availability picture is bounded to providers physically located within that state, with outside referrals treated only as side notes if recorded at all.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because the project is already organized around five state sections, 'service availability for each state' sounds like established reporting language; neither notices that one is thinking about resident access pathways while the other is thinking about geographic inventory boundaries.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to 'confirm the status' of key providers
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'confirm the status' of the higher-interest providers before drafting.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes status is confirmed once a knowledgeable administrator or clinician says the provider still serves patients in substantially the same way and any notable price point or referral arrangement remains in place.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes status is only truly confirmed when the callback sheet is fully updated with current fee range, procedure category, and whether the site is active, referral-only, or inactive.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both care about accuracy, and 'confirm the status' sounds softer and more conversational than a formal survey term like 'verification,' so the different completion thresholds remain hidden beneath apparent agreement.

misalignment_points.topic: What the first 'state summary draft' is supposed to be
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that Rafael will prepare the first 'state summary draft.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means a readable narrative overview for each state highlighting access patterns, major cost barriers, urban-rural gaps, and any striking exceptions that she can use in briefing materials.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means a structured draft package consisting mainly of cleaned provider tables, categorized listings, and brief notes generated from the survey file.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both use the phrase 'state summary draft' as if it were already familiar, and each version plausibly counts as a draft summary in this kind of project, so neither feels a need to spell out the expected format.

What I need from Rafael is a concise, readable set of state pieces that highlight real access patterns, costs, and a few persuasive examples.
